list.listitem: Abnormal tooth wear, orofacial pain, temporomandibular joint (TMJ) sounds, and difficulty closing the mouth support the diagnosis. C
Occlusal mouth splints are the mainstay of treatment for sleep bruxism to protect teeth from damage, but they do not decrease episodes of bruxism. B
Mandibular advancement device mouth splints decrease episodes of sleep bruxism but are uncomfortable to wear. C
Clonidine or clonazepam are effective in reducing bruxism but are considered second-line treatments. C

background.definition: Bruxism is nonfunctional jaw movement that includes clenching, grinding, clicking, and gnashing of the teeth, most commonly occurring during sleep.

list.listitem: Prevalence in children is 14% to 20%.
Prevalence in adults is 8%, but decreases with age. Roughly 3% of patients older than 60 years do not resolve completely.
One in 5 sleep bruxers report concomitant orofacial pain.
Bruxism is classified into primary (idiopathic) or secondary (iatrogenic).
Some of the common secondary causes seen in clinical practice include Down's syndrome, Parkinson's disease, and anxiety disorders.
Amphetamines, selective-serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and levodopa drugs have all been implicated in causing secondary bruxism.
Bruxism is suspected to be multifactorial, with disruption of the serotonergic modulation of dopamine neurons in the mesocortical tract serving as a major contributor based on anecdotal case reports.

Rhythmic masticatory muscle activity is characterized by repetitive jaw muscle contractions occurring in 60% of normal adults while asleep without associated tooth grinding. Patients with bruxism have more frequent and exaggerated muscle activity.
Clinical diagnosis is most reliably made using history of tooth-grinding noise from bed partner. C
Abnormal tooth wear, orofacial pain, TMJ sounds, and difficulty closing the mouth are the most reliable signs of bruxism. C
Formal diagnostic testing with polysomnography is useful only to rule out associated conditions such as sleep apnea when suggested by the patient's history. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Dyskinetic posturing associated with vocalizations during sleep; form of epilepsy
Sensation of choking or dyspnea during sleep; no grinding of teeth
Rapid jaw jerks or twitches as compared with more sustained jaw closure in bruxism
Pain over the TMJ; associated with popping/clicking in bruxism

list.listitem: Bruxing episodes are typically reported by the patient's sleep partner who notices grinding and/or clicking noises. Symptoms related to bruxism include pain or abnormal sounds of the TMJ, craniofacial pain, morning headaches, and difficulties with mouth movements, more specifically difficulty closing the mouth.

TMJ symptoms provide the strongest evidence of ongoing bruxism. In a study of 483 Italian adults from the general population, 4% of whom reported bruxism, there was an independent association between bruxism and orofacial muscle pain (OR 1.8), TMJ sounds such as clicking or popping (OR 1.6), and difficulty closing the mouth (OR 2.8).
There is conflicting evidence linking stress to bruxism.

Abnormal tooth wear of the incisors is not significantly associated with bruxism (OR 1.1) but can be associated with other causes such as holding drinks in the mouth before swallowing. Masseter muscle hypertrophy, tooth indentation of the tongue, and jaw malocclusion, including anterior overbite, correlate poorly with bruxism.

Numerous methods for the assessment of bruxism are reported in the literature, including portable electromyographic devices, force measuring devices, dental examinations, and questionnaires. None of these modalities have been well validated in the clinical setting.

Polysomnographic recording (sleep studies) can confirm the diagnosis of bruxism (sensitivity 72%, specificity 94%) but are most helpful in ruling out associated disorders such as obstructive sleep apnea, periodic leg movements, and epilepsy.
Obtain a history from patient and parent or sleep partner of tooth grinding or tapping. Look for abnormal tooth wear or jaw muscle discomfort on examination.
Not all patients require treatment—it depends on the severity of symptoms. Diagnostic testing is only recommended to rule out associated conditions such as sleep apnea.
Dental treatment with a mandibular advancement device decreases bruxing episodes, but discomfort while wearing the device limits compliance. C
Occlusal appliances protect teeth from damage but do not decrease the number of bruxing episodes. B
Pharmacotherapy with clonidine or clonazepam may provide a short-term decrease in bruxing episodes, but evidence on reduced pain and improved sleep is lacking. C
Botulinum toxin injections may be helpful in severe bruxism. C
Behavioral therapies can decrease daytime jaw clenching but have little effect on sleep bruxism. C

Pharmacologic treatment is considered second-line therapy for treatment of bruxism and is recommended only when associated pain is intense enough to affect quality of life or in individuals with a concern for significant dental injury.
Clonidine 0.3 mg given at bedtime decreases episodes of sleep bruxism (NNT 3.2), but with significant side effects including hypotension and loss of rapid eye movement sleep.
Clonazepam 1 mg at bedtime has also been shown to decrease sleep-related bruxism.
Studies looking at L-dopa, amitriptyline, bromocriptine, propranolol, and tryptophan have shown no benefit for the treatment of bruxism.
Solid evidence for pharmacologic therapy for reducing pain and improving sleep and quality of life is lacking.
In children with sleep apnea, removal of the tonsils and adenoids can eliminate bruxism.
Botulinum toxin injections in the masseter muscles every 3 to 6 months can be used as a last resort in patients with severe symptoms who are unresponsive to standard therapies.

A systematic review of 14 studies with only 395 patients, but only a minority of studies could be used for meta-analysis. The pain reduction at 1 and 3 months but not 6 months were significantly lower than for placebo.

Mandibular advancement devices advance the lower jaw forward slightly and are primarily used to treat sleep apnea. These devices have also been shown to reduce sleep bruxism (NNT 2.2). However, they are associated with jaw discomfort, which may limit patient compliance.
Occlusal mouth splints worn at night protect teeth from fracture and pulpitis, but there is insufficient evidence to show an actual reduction in bruxing episodes.

A systematic review identified 15 studies comparing different kinds of splints, andn concluded that adjustable splints (such as full-occlusion biofeedback splints) reduced sleep bruxism and improved symptoms and overall well-being more than alternatives.
Physical therapy is effective in improving pain and jaw function in patients presenting with myofascial pain of the head and neck related to bruxism.
Behavioral therapy with biofeedback and relaxation can decrease daytime jaw clenching but has little effect on sleep bruxism.
All patients should be referred to a dentist early, whether or not symptomatic, to evaluate for secondary dental causes and to assess for abnormal tooth wear requiring treatment.
Bruxism leads to accelerated tooth wear, which can result in hypersensitivity, tooth fracture, or failure of dental implants. C
Although bruxism is associated with sleep microarousals, patients have been found to have normal sleep architecture and efficiency. B
Consequences of chronic untreated bruxism include morning headaches; myofascial pain in the neck, back, and shoulders; and TMJ pain. B
Bruxism decreases with age and may resolve completely if a secondary cause is identified and treated. C
Bruxism is much more common in children but decreases with age and often disappears with the eruption of secondary dentition.

In most instances, childhood bruxism is mild and requires no treatment. However, in the absence of significant symptoms, a dental evaluation should still be performed to look for signs of tooth damage requiring treatment.
